source.title: FalseReject: A Resource for Improving Contextual Safety and Mitigating Over-Refusals in LLMs via Structured Reasoning
source.authors: Zhe-Hao Zhang; Weijie Xu; Wu Fanyou; Chandan K. Reddy

record.tranche_reason: Measures per-token KL using the approach attributed to Qi et al. (2024) and tests prefilling and other jailbreak attacks, reporting results on models fine-tuned with FalseReject.
record.gate_note: The study does not test harmful-example fine-tuning or ordinary benign instruction fine-tuning alone. It does test fine-tuning with FalseReject, a targeted benign contextual-safety dataset mixed with utility data, and reports harmful-prompt attack success rates. For the per-token KL analysis, the paper describes qualitative results but the plotted values are figure-only. Rows from Table 2 for general utility and over-refusal metrics are not included because they do not measure harmful-request compliance named by these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains base models with utility data plus FalseReject contextual-safety data and reports two things: Qi-style per-token KL depth curves (figure-only, described in text) and prefilling, GCG and AutoDAN ASR (Table 5). These bear on V4 (attacks bypass refusal in these models) and V7 (whether the claimed deeper alignment resists prefilling). It is a new setting: SFT from base with targeted data, KL measured on FalseReject refusal responses rather than harmful prompts. It does not test V2. No safety-aligned model is fine-tuned on benign data; both arms start from the base model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that FalseReject SFT cuts over-refusal without hurting safety or utility, and improves safety in reasoning models. They read the KL curves as deeper, more sustained alignment. They report slightly lower or equal jailbreak ASR, which they take as support for structured reasoning fostering deeper alignment.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SFT on base pretrained models with 12,000 utility pairs and 1,300 FalseReject pairs at a 90:10 utility-to-safety ratio; the KL measurement follows the cited prior approach, but the training data and intervention differ. Training uses three epochs.
record.method_sensitivity: The depth analysis compares three model families and their official instruction-tuned versions. Jailbreak ASR differs by model and attack method; all reported FalseReject-tuned ASRs are lower than their utility-only baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: Reasoning models SFT'd from base on OpenThoughts alone have low safety (AdvBench USR 17–67%). Adding FalseReject-CoT restores it to about 100%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reasoning-only SFT from base yields weak refusal; adding safety reasoning data restores it (not erosion of an existing alignment).

record.problems: KL results are presented as curves with qualitative textual descriptions and no numerical per-position values. Jailbreak evaluation uses 200 harmful prompts and reports no uncertainty estimates. The fine-tuning comparison uses a targeted contextual-safety dataset mixed with utility data, so it does not establish the effect of ordinary benign fine-tuning alone.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant attack result rows were omitted. Table 5 marks Gemma-2-2B GCG results with dashes, so no result row was created for that condition.

untested.parts: No benign fine-tuning of an already safety-aligned model. Both arms are trained from base.
KL on harmful prompts is not measured. The official-instruct curves on FalseReject refusals are figure-only, with no position-wise values.
Decoding-parameter attacks are not tested; GCG was not run on Gemma-2-2B.
The cause of shallowness is not isolated.
No adaptive attacks and no harmful fine-tuning attacks. Depth is not measured on harmful prompts.

missing.what: No-attack harmful-prompt safety (AdvBench/MI/SR/SB USR-toxic) for the Tulu baseline and +FalseReject models. This is the needed baseline showing attacks, including prefilling, raise ASR from about 0%.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 challenges label is wrong: there is no benign fine-tuning of an aligned model. The reader's V3 challenges label is wrong: KL is not on harmful prompts and is confounded by the training data. The reader's V4 limits_scope label conflates the FalseReject-vs-baseline comparison with whether attacks bypass safety. R1–R11 states listed are the V7 states; for V4 all are observed.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning with harmful examples and resulting harmful-request compliance.
Ordinary benign instruction data alone; the study uses FalseReject contextual-safety data mixed with utility data.
The KL analysis is on refusal responses from FalseReject and reports qualitative curve descriptions, not numeric per-position values.
Decoding changes; the attacks tested are GCG, prefilling, and AutoDAN variants.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
The study proposes that structured reasoning fosters deeper alignment, but does not isolate or establish what causes shallow alignment.
The study evaluates its trained models on selected jailbreak attacks, not whether deeper alignment holds across other attacks, prompts, or training conditions.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: GCG adversarial-suffix attack; ASR on harmful prompts, comparing utility-only tuning with FalseReject added

conditions.value: 200 harmful prompts sampled from Zou et al. (2023)

rows.note: Both conditions have nonzero ASR; the FalseReject-tuned model has lower ASR.
rows.check: Not V2: both arms are SFT from base, and Tulu-3 itself contains safety data, so nothing erodes an existing alignment. For V4 the relevant baseline is no-attack harmful compliance (Table 2 AdvBench USR 100%, about 0% harmful), not Tulu-only. Against that, GCG reaches 45.5% ASR, so V4 is observed. The partial state is for V7: the GCG reduction is small (51.5 to 45.5).

relationships.condition: Prefilling and other jailbreaks after FalseReject tuning
relationships.reason: Despite the claimed deeper alignment, prefilling ASR stays 27.5–48.5% (R2, R6, R9). Several attack drops are 0.5–1 point (R5, R7, R8, R9). The deeper KL does not yield prefilling robustness.

relation.reason: Section 5.2 directly examines alignment depth using the cited KL approach; Appendix E measures prefilling and suffix-attack success.

tranche.reason: Tests alignment depth and jailbreak robustness in a new contextual-safety SFT setting, using different training data and model families.

source_check.notes: Table 2 USR_Toxic includes safe partial compliance as well as direct refusal; near-perfect USR is not a direct refusal rate. Table 5 reports no uncertainty or significance tests, and Section 5.2 does not specify the KL sample's split.

statements.correction: Section 5.2: 1,000 FalseReject instruction-response pairs; responses classified as refusals; sample split unspecified. Table 5: FalseReject prefilling ASR Qwen2.5-7B 27.5%, Llama-3.2-1B 31.5%, Gemma-2-2B 48.5%.
statements.problem: The FalseReject findings and ASRs are correct, but the text does not identify the KL sample as training responses or establish training-split overlap.

statements.correction: KL measured on 1,000 FalseReject instruction-response pairs with responses classified as refusals; training/test split unspecified; no harmful-continuation recovery measurement in Figure 4.
statements.problem: The limitation of the KL measure is sound, but calling the measured responses refusal-training responses asserts provenance the paper does not specify.
